title: When should two microservices be MERGED back (or decomposition stop): when the boundary creates coordination without autonomy (same team, deployed together, synchronous chains, shared consistency, lockstep schema/API changes), and why should a healthy architecture be able to delete/merge services, not only create them?
shortTitle: When should two microservices be merged back
keyPoints: Merge two services back when the boundary produces coordination without autonomy.
Signal 1: same team owns both and nearly every feature touches both.
Signal 2: lockstep deployment: you can never deploy one without the other.
Signal 3: synchronous request chain where A cannot function without B being up.
Signal 4: shared consistency requirement forcing distributed transactions for simple operations.
Signal 5: lockstep schema or API changes where changing one always forces a change in the other.
A healthy architecture treats merging and deleting services as first-class operations, not just creating them.

s1_definition.oneliner: Merge two services back when the boundary causes coordination without autonomy, such as shared team, lockstep deploys, synchronous chains, shared consistency, and lockstep schema changes, and treat deleting or merging services as a normal, healthy operation.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Coordination without autonomy** – the boundary adds network hops and operational cost without granting independent deployment.
- **Signal 1** – same team owns both; nearly every feature touches both services.
- **Signal 2** – lockstep deployment: never deployed one without the other.
- **Signal 3** – synchronous chain: A calls B for every request; A is useless when B is down.
- **Signal 4** – shared consistency: a simple operation requires a distributed transaction.
- **Signal 5** – lockstep schema/API changes: changing one always forces a coordinated change in the other.
- **Healthy architecture** – merging and deleting services is a first-class operation, not a failure.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine two departments were split apart, but they share one manager, always submit budgets together, constantly phone each other to finish a single task, must balance the same ledger, and can never change a form without the other changing the same form on the same day. They are not really two departments; they are one department pretending to be two, with couriers running pointlessly between them. The healthy move is to merge them back.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Five Signals to Merge:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Signal 1: Same team, shared changes     │
  │  Signal 2: Always deployed together      │
  │  Signal 3: Synchronous chain (A->B)      │
  │  Signal 4: Shared consistency needed     │
  │  Signal 5: Lockstep schema/API changes   │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Before merge:                            │
  │  Transfer Svc ──REST──> LimitCheck Svc   │
  │  2 repos, 2 pipelines, 2 DBs, 2 deploys │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                     │ merge
                     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  After merge:                             │
  │  TransferService.checkLimit() (in-process)│
  │  1 repo, 1 pipeline, 1 DB, 1 deploy      │
  │  Fewer hops, simpler, more resilient      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Knowing when to merge services back is just as important as knowing when to split them, and most engineers only learn the splitting half. Two microservices should be merged when the boundary produces coordination without autonomy: same team with shared changes, lockstep deploys, synchronous chains where one cannot work without the other, shared consistency forcing distributed transactions, and lockstep schema changes.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj once split a limit-check service from the transfer service. Every single transfer made a blocking call to it, so when limit-check was down no transfer could proceed. The two services shared one availability fate. Merging turned a fragile distributed check into one resilient local method call with identical business logic.

The deeper principle is that a healthy architecture must be able to delete and merge services, not only create them. The correct number of services is not the maximum; it is whatever maximizes autonomy. Boundaries are hypotheses, and a mature team revises a wrong hypothesis by merging back without ego.

Remember one sentence: merge two services back when the boundary creates coordination without autonomy, because the right number of services is whatever maximizes team independence, not the maximum possible.
